story:
Thoth, a moon deity depicted as ibis-headed or baboon-headed, served as scribe and counselor to the sun god Ra, standing beside him on his solar barque alongside the goddess Ma'at, truth and order personified, who was also his wife. Thoth invented writing and hieroglyphs, and was credited with authoring works of science, religion, magic and law.

In one myth, the year originally had only 360 days, and the sky goddess Nut was unable to bear children during that year. Thoth gambled with the moon for a portion of its light—one seventy-second of it, equal to five days—and won. During these five additional days, Nut and the earth god Geb gave birth to four deities: Osiris, Set, Isis, and Nephthys.

Later, when Osiris was killed, Thoth gave Isis the magic words needed to restore her dead husband, enabling her to conceive a son, Horus. After a battle between Horus and Set, Thoth offered counsel and wisdom to resolve their conflict.

In the underworld, Thoth appeared in the form of an ape, serving as the god of equilibrium, who reported when the scale weighing the heart of the deceased against a feather representing truth balanced exactly even, determining the judgment of the dead.

In another tale, Thoth demonstrated a new invention, writing, to King Thamus, praising it as a remedy for memory. The king replied that writing would not strengthen memory but only remind, giving people the appearance of wisdom without its substance, since they would hear much without being properly taught.
